en: Petavatthu,
Cūḷavagga 1.
The Story of the Non-Sinking Ghost (Abhijjamānapetavatthu)
“While the waters of the Ganges flow here, you go across them naked,
like a preta from the past.”
“Wearing garlands and adorned,
where will you go, O ghost,
and where will your dwelling be?”
“I shall go to Cundaṭṭhila,” the peta says,
“between here and Vāsabhagāma.”
And [he was] near Vārāṇasī.
Having seen him, the high minister known as Koliya—
I gave roasted flour, cooked rice,
and a pair of yellow garments to a peta while standing upon a boat.
She had it given to the barber;
when it was given to the barber,
it appeared to the peta at that very spot.
Then, wearing fine garments,
adorned with garlands and ornaments,
[he appeared] before the peta standing in his place.
May this offering be of benefit;
therefore, out of compassion, one should give to the departed again and again.
Some wearing grass garments,
others wearing hair-cloths—
the hungry ghosts go forth seeking food.
They depart in every direction.
Some, having run far,
turn back even without having found [the goal].
Fainting, bewildered, and reeling,
they fell down upon the ground;
and having fallen there, they remained.
They have been cast down upon the ground;
having failed to perform wholesome deeds in the past,
they are like things scorched by fire in the heat of the sun.
“Formerly we were of evil character,
householders and mothers of families;
even while there were things to be given, we— ”
They scattered abundant food and drink even upon themselves as a lamp for their own sake.
To those who had gone forth on the right path,
we gave nothing at all; we were inactive,
lazy, and unwilling to work.
Desiring fine food, we were extravagant;
as givers of mouthfuls and morsels,
we reviled those who received them.
Those houses, those maidservants, and those very ornaments are now enjoyed by others.
We are partakers of suffering.
The weaver is held in contempt, as is the chariot-maker and the potter.
They become outcasts and wretched men,
and repeatedly barbers;
whatever [tasks] are lowly, they perform them.
And into wretched families;
they are born in those very places—
this is the destiny of the miserly.
Those who have performed wholesome deeds in the past,
who are generous and free from stinginess,
fill the heavenly realms.
They illuminate Nandana,
and having enjoyed themselves in the Vejayanta palace according to their desires;
Having passed away from those states of enjoyment, they are born into high-born families in gabled houses and palaces.
On couches spread with woolen rugs,
their limbs fanned by peacock-feather whisks,
they were high-born and renowned.
They go from lap to lap,
adorned girls wearing garlands;
nurses stand waiting upon them.
Seeking happiness in the evening and at dawn—
this is not for those who have not performed merit;
this is only for those who have performed merit.
The sorrowless, joyful, and delightful Great Forest of the Thirty-three gods is a place of happiness for those who have performed meritorious deeds.
There is no happiness here or in the next world for those who have not performed merit; but for those who have performed merit,
there is happiness both here and in the next world.
For those who desire companionship with them,
much wholesome merit must be performed;
for it is those who have done meritorious deeds that rejoice.
“Possessing enjoyments in heaven.
Thus ends the first *Abhijjamāna-peta-vatthu*.
